entities.name: Chera dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Chera dynasty, one of the three great classical Tamil kingdoms of ancient southern India (along with the Chola and Pandya dynasties), ruled the regions of present-day Kerala and western Tamil Nadu from approximately the 3rd century BCE to the 12th century CE — a remarkable continuity spanning over 1,500 years across two distinct periods (Early Cheras, 3rd c. BCE - 5th c. CE; Later Cheras/Kulashekhara, 800-1102 CE). The Cheras were the dominant power of the Malabar Coast (modern Kerala), controlling the lucrative spice trade that connected Rome, Arabia, and China to South Asia.

The Early Cheras' capital Vanchi (possibly modern Karur, Tamil Nadu) traded with the Roman Empire: the 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea' (1st century CE) describes the Malabar Coast's pepper, cardamom, and ivory trade with Rome; the Tabula Peutingeriana (medieval copy of a Roman road map) shows a 'Temple of Augustus' at Muciri (Muzuris, Kerala) — evidence of permanent Roman presence in Chera territory. The 'Peutingeriana' evidence suggests Roman merchants established permanent trading posts in Chera lands, making it one of the earliest documented East-West commercial relationships.

The Later Cheras (Kulashekhara dynasty, 800-1102 CE), based in Mahodayapuram (Kodungallur), patronized Malayalam literature, built Kerala's great temples (including the Vadakkunnathan Temple, Thrissur), and facilitated the Nambudiri Brahmin settlement that created Kerala's unique religious and caste structure. Their final defeat by the Chola Empire (1102 CE) ended centralized Chera rule, fragmenting Kerala into the small kingdoms that Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama encountered in 1498.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Chera dynasty — controlling the Malabar Coast spice trade that connected Rome to Asia, documented in Roman sources 2,000 years ago, and establishing Malayalam literature and Kerala's temple tradition — shaped global trade history and remains Kerala's foundational political and cultural institution.
